records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. RHS's single-species profile carries the subtitle 'Virginian witch hazel' under its 'Hamamelis virginiana' heading, and its Other common names field reads 'American witch hazel, snapping hazel nut, spotted alder, winter bloom'. MoBot's single-species page displays a single Common Name field reading 'common witch hazel'; a longer Common Names list sits behind a popup whose text exists only in the link's overlib attribute markup, so it is not quoted here. NC State's Common Name(s) field stacks five entries -- Common Witchhazel, Common Witch Hazel, Southern Witch Hazel, Witch Hazel, Witch-Hazel -- in the same order as its page-title parenthetical, so its first entry is 'Common Witchhazel'; NC State's body prose opens 'Witch hazel is a deciduous shrub or small tree in the witch hazel family (Hamamelidaceae) native to eastern North America (including North Carolina), where it may be found growing along woodland margins and stream banks.' 'Witch Hazel' alone is a genus-umbrella name: RHS's genus guide states the genus Hamamelis is 'Commonly known as witch hazel,' so it is excluded as a species-distinguishing lead. common_name is set to 'Common Witch Hazel', the title-cased form of MoBot's single-value Common Name field and NC State's second stacked entry, over RHS's 'Virginian witch hazel' and NC State's one-word first entry 'Common Witchhazel'.
unknowns: toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail left null: no admissible source addresses toxicity to cats or dogs for Hamamelis virginiana. NC State's Plant Type field tags the species 'Edible' with no 'Poisonous' tag and no Poison block on the page, so absence of evidence was treated as unknown rather than assumed safe.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max left null: NC State's pH field is the open-ended 'Acid (<6.0)' band (no closed floor or ceiling to read a number from), and RHS's pH field is the categorical 'Acid or Neutral' rather than a numeric range, so no ceiling or floor could be derived per the pH-band rule.

water_regime left null: the only watering-scale data found, MoBot's structured 'Water: Medium' field, is mid-scale and cannot support keep_moist on its own per the rules; no admissible source gave an explicit watering statement for this species, so it is disclosed only as a counterpoint, not used to set the field.

water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis left null per the in-ground-shrub rule: no admissible source framed watering for this species with a day interval or a dry-down depth.

day_f_min/max, night_f_min/max, chill_damage_f, cool_rest_note left null: this is a fully hardy outdoor shrub (NC State lists USDA zones 3a-9b) and no admissible source states a numeric temperature range or a frost/chill damage onset temperature.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State carries a Poison block (Plant Type includes "Poisonous"): Poison Severity is High. Poison Symptoms: "The toxic principle interferes with normal skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle, and nerve function. Clinical effects typically occur within a few hours after ingestion, and can include acute digestive upset, excessive drooling, loss of appetite, frequent bowel movements/diarrhea, colic, sweating, abdominal pain, depression, weakness, loss of coordination, stupor, watering of eyes and nose, nausea, cardiac failure, vomiting, leg paralysis, weak heart rate, and recumbency for 2 or more days; at this point, improvement may be seen or the animal may become comatose and die. Typically not very palatable to horses unless it is the only forage available, but sheep and goats may graze readily on the plant." Poison Toxic Principle: "Andromedotoxin, a resinoid; arbutin, a glycoside, Grayanotoxins." Causes Contact Dermatitis: No. Poison Part (full list): Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Seeds, Stems. This severity rating and symptom list are from NC State's human-scoped Poison block; separately, its Problems tags list "Poisonous to Humans," "Problem for Cats," "Problem for Dogs," and "Problem for Horses" as co-listed, distinct tags. RHS (a different, cat/dog-scoped source) states the plant is "Harmful if eaten" and specifically warns "Pets (dogs, cats, rabbits, tortoises): Harmful if eaten," and separately carries a handling warning: "Wear gloves and other protective equipment when handling."

records.name_note: Sources disagree on which name is 'the' common name because 'serviceberry' alone is applied across the genus rather than to this species -- NC State's Amelanchier arborea page lists the bare 'Serviceberry' among that species' common names too, while MoBot and RHS both give the bare 'serviceberry' for A. canadensis. NC State's Common Name(s) field for A. canadensis stacks seven entries (Canadian Serviceberry, Eastern Serviceberry, Juneberry, Serviceberry, Shadblow serviceberry, Shadbush, Shadbush Serviceberry); the list is alphabetized and matches the page-title parenthetical's order, so its first entry is an alphabetical position, not a designated primary. That same page's Description instead opens 'Shadblow serviceberry is a deciduous, early-flowering, large shrub or small tree...'. MoBot's displayed Common Name field carries the single value 'serviceberry'; a longer common-names list exists only inside an overlib link attribute and is therefore not quoted here, but MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics prose calls the plant 'commonly called shadblow serviceberry.' RHS's plant-profile subtitle and page title are likewise the bare 'serviceberry,' and its Other common names field reads 'grape pear, juneberry, shadblow, shadbush' -- no 'shadblow serviceberry' compound. Because the bare 'serviceberry' is not species-distinguishing, the compound used in both NC State's and MoBot's own species-page prose, 'Shadblow Serviceberry,' is taken as the lead common_name. Naming here is further tangled with A. arborea and A. laevis: Clemson HGIC's Serviceberry factsheet -- whose main subject is Downy serviceberry (A. arborea) -- covers this species as a run-in entry under 'Related Species & Cultivars,' headed 'Amelanchier canadensis (Shadblow Serviceberry):', and states it 'is distinctly different in habit from the A. arborea and A. laevis,' blooming 'about a week after A. arborea.' NC State's A. arborea page leads its Description with 'Downy serviceberry,' and its own alphabetized list runs Alabama Serviceberry, Downy Serviceberry, Juneberries, Serviceberry, Service-tree, Shadblow, Shadbush -- including the bare 'Shadblow' but not the compound 'Shadblow Serviceberry,' underscoring that the short names overlap across species while the compound used here is specific to A. canadensis.

records.name_note: 'Pinxterbloom Azalea' is the lead common name on both North American sources. NC State's Common Name(s) list runs Pinxterbloom Azalea, Pinxter Flower, Wild Azalea, and its first entry matches the first name in the page-title parenthetical 'Rhododendron periclymenoides (Pinxterbloom Azalea, Pinxter Flower, Wild Azalea)'; NC State's body prose likewise opens 'Pinxterbloom azalea is a deciduous, woody shrub...'. MoBot's Common Name field carries the single value 'pinxterbloom azalea' (a two-name list sits only in the link's attribute markup and is not quoted). The auditor found an RHS profile for this species displaying 'Pinxter flower'; no URL for it is in this record, so it is noted rather than cited. No admissible page uses the name 'pink azalea'. Older sources file the species under the synonym Rhododendron nudiflorum: NC State's 'Previously known as:' field gives 'Rhododendron nudiflorum', and MoBot's Noteworthy Characteristics paragraph states 'Synonymous with and formerly known as R. nudiflorum.'
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Poison block (filed under the human-scoped 'Poisonous to Humans' heading) rates Poison Severity: Low, and its Poison Symptoms field states 'While the plants are known to contain toxins, ingestion of moderate amounts of azalea (nectar or leaves) poses little toxic hazard.' The Poison Toxic Principle is Grayanotoxins, and the plant does not cause contact dermatitis (Causes Contact Dermatitis: No). The full Poison Part list is Bark, Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Sap/Juice, Stems. Separately from the human-scoped Poison block, NC State's structured Problems tags also mark the plant Problem for Cats, Problem for Dogs, and Problem for Horses, and its Plant Type list co-lists the trait Poisonous alongside Native Plant, Perennial, Shrub, and Woody Plant. No admissible source gives a cat/dog-specific symptom list separate from the human-scoped one above.
unknowns: soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max left null: NC State's only pH tag is the open-ended band 'Acid (<6.0)', which per instructions supplies no floor or ceiling; no RHS page exists to cross-check a closed-band reading.

water_regime left null: no admissible source frames watering for this species as a keep-moist/dry-down statement. MoBot's structured field reads 'Water: Medium' (mid-scale, disclosed here only as a counterpoint, not used to set the field), and NC State's only related guidance is the general caution 'Avoid overwatering and over-fertilizing,' which is not a watering regime statement.
